newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to visit flood victims in North Dakota.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to visit flood victims in North Dakota.

text.p: President Clinton will visit flood-ravaged North Dakota Tuesday and is expected to tour the region by helicopter and to meet victims of the storm damage, the White House said Monday.

Clinton plans to fly into Grand Forks, which has been hit badly by the flooding, and is expected to meet people who have lost their homes and are being housed temporarily at the Grand Forks Air Force Base.

This weekend, the Red River punched through clay dikes and swept into the North Dakota city. A devastating fire followed, tearing through the downtown business district as several feet of water kept firefighters from doing their job.
Clinton typically tries to avoid visiting disaster areas while relief efforts are getting started so as not to disrupt the rescue and clean-up work.

Asked if a presidential visit, which typically diverts local resources for his transportation and security, might disrupt the efforts, White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn replied: "What we want to do is make certain that we don't.

"That's why we're going to Grand Forks Air Force Base, which is where a bunch of these victims are housed right now," she added. "Of course we wouldn't do anything that would impact on any of the relief efforts."
"It's slighly earlier than normal, but these people are facing a disaster and we want to see what we can do to help as soon as possible," she said.
Clinton's helicopter tour is likely to take in both North Dakota and Minnesota, the White House said.
The president is still on crutches since tearing a tendon in his right knee March 14 and has not taken a helicopter since because of the difficulty getting up the stairs.

Glynn said he was expected to use a small helicopter with one step Tuesday, adding his recovery from knee surgery is going well. "He doing better," she said. "He is more mobile; he can move his knee 90 degrees now. He's ahead of schedule."

Earlier, White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton was monitoring the situation closely and was receiving frequent updates from James Lee Witt, the director of the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

"FEMA has got 500 people out there already and another 100 that are arriving shortly to deal with the flood damage," McCurry said. "The president's been getting regular updates...(It's) obviously a very difficult situation."
